title: The AI Imperative: Reshaping of the Legal Industry
author: Deloitte Legal

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Deloitte accepts the cluster’s central claim that organisational absorption—not technology procurement alone—determines whether legal departments capture AI gains. It materially develops that proposition with survey evidence on strategy and QA gaps, a foundations-to-scaling transformation roadmap, and concrete recommendations spanning operating-model redesign, legal engineering, workforce development, governance and transparent sharing of efficiency gains with outside counsel. It also carefully distinguishes anticipated savings and staffing changes from benefits already realised.
qs: That means bringing clients into the conversation on deployment, co-developing approaches where appropriate, and demonstrating transparency on how efficiency gains are being reflected in pricing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Deloitte accepts the cluster’s core view that AI value depends on selective workflow deployment, human oversight and operating-model redesign rather than technology procurement alone. It materially extends that proposition with survey evidence on immature value realisation and quality assurance, plus a concrete three-stage transformation roadmap spanning foundations, workflow embedding and organisational scaling.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Deloitte broadly endorses the cluster’s proposition: AI is reorganising routine legal work and workforce composition more clearly than replacing lawyers wholesale, while realised gains depend on governance, quality assurance, training, workflow redesign and balanced organisational investment. It also directly recognises the apprenticeship risk created when AI absorbs junior work and recommends structured alternatives for developing judgement.

kp.k: Survey evidence concerns corporate legal departments
kp.d: Deloitte and RSGI surveyed 121 senior legal leaders through an online questionnaire between April and May 2026, covering departments from below 25 FTE to over 200 FTE across industries and the Americas, APAC, EMEA and UK & Ireland. Qualitative law-firm interviews supplement the survey; the analysis and commentary are Deloitte’s own. Findings about law firms should therefore be distinguished from the survey evidence about their corporate clients.

kp.k: Adoption has advanced beyond pilots
kp.d: Figure 5 reports 31% in initial deployment, 30% scaling deployment, 10% fully embedded, 27% experimenting or piloting, and 2% with no adoption. Thus 71% are at initial deployment or beyond; the report’s separate 61% deployment figure excludes fully embedded respondents. The report compares this with 76% reporting no adoption in its 2024 survey.
qs: 71% of respondents have moved beyond no adoption, piloting and experimentation

kp.k: Investment grows, but technology dominates
kp.d: 79% of departments report increased AI investment; among those reporting an increase, budgets grew an average 67% year on year. Technology and infrastructure is the highest investment area for 67%, while training and transformation rank third and fourth. Deloitte argues that people, process redesign, data and cultural change require protected investment rather than being treated as follow-on activities after procurement.
qs: 79% of legal departments report their AI investment has
grown by an average of 67% year-on-year for those reporting
Technology investment leads while Transformation lags

kp.k: Strategy and quality assurance lag deployment
kp.d: Across respondents, 52% have a formal department AI strategy, 34% defined KPIs and metrics, 68% governance or risk frameworks, and only 24% quality-assurance frameworks. Among high-maturity respondents—scaling or fully embedded—the corresponding figures are 64%, 56%, 82% and 33%. Deloitte warns that missing use-case-level QA becomes more consequential as complex workflows and agents increase error costs and make consistent human checking harder to embed.
qs: defined review checkpoints and feedback loops.

kp.k: Buying leads, while consumption complicates cost control
kp.d: Legal departments allocate approximately 62% of AI technology budgets to buying and 38% to building. Deloitte reports that enterprise build capability, security requirements and data retention favour internal development, while rapid third-party platform improvement favours buying. Vibe coding makes local prototyping easier, but consumption-based token and API charges create governance and cost-control requirements. Some respondents cannot identify their investment levels, weakening ROI tracking.
qs: Approximately 62% of AI technology budgets are allocated
A significant proportion of respondents flagged their AI

kp.k: Document-intensive work leads practical adoption
kp.d: Contracts and commercial leads practice-area adoption, with 67% at initial deployment or beyond. Document review, summarisation and comparison is the most mature activity, with approximately 50% scaling or fully embedded. More advanced activities remain less adopted: Figure 7 shows no adoption for 64% in direct AI-generated legal advice, 65% in predictive litigation analytics and 48% in outside-counsel management and spend analytics.
qs: Predictive analytics in litigation (e.g. early case assessment)

kp.k: Automation expectations create competing uses for capacity
kp.d: Respondents expect AI to save or automate an average 28% of legal department work over the next 2–3 years, rather than reporting this as an achieved result. Expected potential is 34% in contracts and commercial, 32% in legal operations, 29% in regulatory and compliance, and 19% in antitrust and competition. Deloitte identifies alternative uses for capacity: insourcing, higher-value work, absorbing demand without hiring, or reducing team costs. The report cites insourcing as a priority for 66% in several places and 65% in the automation discussion.
qs: an average of 28% of legal department

kp.k: Expected benefits extend beyond efficiency
kp.d: Productivity and cost reduction dominate respondents’ priorities, but Deloitte argues that knowledge-grounded advice, broader document coverage and predictive analytics could improve business decisions and risk management. Half of high-maturity respondents, versus 38% overall, anticipate direct AI-generated client advice as transformational over the next 2–3 years. This is an expectation of greater autonomy, not evidence that unsupervised advice is already widespread; Deloitte stresses guardrails and governance.
qs: half of high maturity respondents (38% across all respondents).

kp.k: Case studies report benefits alongside adoption foundations
kp.d: Deloitte reports that a financial-services department deployed legal AI assistance and translation tools to 1,200 professionals, achieved 75%+ adoption in the first weeks and 5–8% productivity gains in drafting and review. An insurance claims redesign reportedly reduced external spend by 6million Euros annually through automated initial assessment and earlier settlement decisions. An AmLaw30 firm’s programme reached more than 1,000 lawyers and over 85% adoption of available AI assistants. These are reported client case outcomes, distinct from survey-wide findings.
qs: firm’s adoption rates of available AI assistant tools to +85%.

kp.k: Agentic experimentation outpaces mature deployment
kp.d: Figure 11 reports 61% experimenting or piloting agentic AI, 17% in initial deployment, 7% scaling, 2% fully embedded and 13% with no adoption. Initial applications include routine business queries, work triage and routing, and contract review. Deloitte defines agents around autonomous decisions and actions within parameters and recommends early governance development. Its statement that only 21% have mature autonomous-agent governance comes from Deloitte’s wider enterprise report, not the legal-department sample.
qs: 21% of enterprise companies report a mature governance

kp.k: Salesforce illustrates agent governance and emerging roles
kp.d: The Salesforce case describes outside-counsel invoice-query support and a live sales-support case-deflection capability. Contract 360 and the Product Legal Request Agent are described prospectively, rather than as completed deployments. Reported safeguards include risk and accuracy testing, permissions validation, disclaimers and governance reviews. Practice AI Leads dedicate 10–20% of their time to adoption, while a new Agent Manager role combines legal expertise, risk management and technical fluency with oversight responsibilities.
qs: one live and one in development
structured risk and accuracy testing, permissions validation

kp.k: Workforce expectations shift toward recomposition and contraction
kp.d: In 2026, 58% expect broadly unchanged team size with material changes in composition, seniority or skills; 20% expect smaller teams, twice the 2024 proportion. Smaller-team expectations are most common in Financial Services, Chemicals & Agriculture and Technology. Deloitte anticipates more strategic work, greater seniority and additional technical roles as routine work is automated. Its illustrated future mix of agents, AI-native lawyers and hybrid specialists is explicitly Deloitte’s view, not a measured workforce distribution.
qs: The proportion expecting smaller teams has doubled
Our view: Future Shape of the Legal Department

kp.k: Future skill priorities combine AI and human capabilities
kp.d: Respondents expect technology and AI literacy to grow in importance for in-house lawyers (96%), followed by adaptability (89%), strategic business thinking (74%), judgement and critical thinking (73%), and relationships and emotional intelligence (70%). Technical legal knowledge is lower at 51%, which Deloitte interprets as becoming table stakes rather than irrelevant. For GCs, technology and AI leadership scores 95%, adaptability 83% and talent development 70%. The report’s 84% figure for organisations not redesigning roles is sourced to Deloitte’s enterprise study, not established as a finding from this legal survey.
qs: 84% of organisations have not yet redesigned roles

kp.k: Deloitte predicts talent repricing and diamond staffing
kp.d: Deloitte predicts falling demand and salaries for routine-work roles traditionally filled by paralegals, trainees and junior associates, while scarce legal engineers and senior relationship-rich specialists are better placed. It envisages movement from the pyramid toward a leaner diamond with fewer junior and senior generalists and a broader hybrid-skilled middle. A customer-service analogy supports its argument that automation increases the complexity and intensity of residual work; clients sending AI first drafts to outside counsel is offered as a legal example.
qs: demand for those roles is likely to fall
The Nature of Work Will Change – Not Just Volume

kp.k: Legal engineering becomes an operating-model capability
kp.d: Deloitte describes legal engineers as combining legal knowledge, process design and technical fluency to translate business needs into workflows and systems. It reports using a hub-and-spoke model and expects legal engineers to standardise QA, maintain knowledge assets, and monitor agent usage and costs. Survey respondents indicate investment in change and delivery capabilities (67%), legal-technical hybrid roles (49%) and risk, ethics and compliance (43%). Deloitte recommends internal development, external partnerships and dedicated career pathways, while predicting that some future lawyers may enter through legal engineering.
qs: Spotlight: The rise of the Legal Engineer

kp.k: Junior formation requires deliberate replacement learning
kp.d: Deloitte asks how juniors will develop judgement if AI absorbs traditional document-intensive training work. Respondents favour continuous education and rotations (68%), simulations and scenario training (63%), and competency rather than PQE-based progression (60%); 32% favour mandatory manual practice without AI. Deloitte recommends separating learning from execution through structured practice, reflection, supervision and redesigned progression, rather than relying on accumulated hours, and urges leaders not to wait for regulators or law schools.
qs: competency progression rather than PQE based progression

kp.k: AI creates mixed sourcing incentives
kp.d: For nearshore and offshore models, 34% expect somewhat increased use, 5% significant increases, 20% decreases and 24% say it is too early to assess. For ALSPs and managed-service providers, 38% expect somewhat increased use, 7% significant increases, 22% decreases and 21% say it is too early to assess. Deloitte argues that AI-enabled shared hubs and providers’ multi-client investment can favour outsourcing, while departments with sufficient internal AI capability may insource work such as contract and invoice review.
qs: Use of ALSP and Managed Service Providers
AI benefits and investments being made by ALSPs across a multi-client spectrum.

kp.k: Clients expect pricing changes and shared savings
kp.d: Clients prioritise provider cost reduction (78%) and improved quality (57%); 85% expect AI to change law-firm pricing to a moderate, large or very large extent. Respondents expect hourly-rate work to fall from 72% to 44% within 2–3 years, while 42% favour equal sharing of AI-generated cost savings. Deloitte reports some GCs setting 20–40% cost-reduction targets over 2–3 years; the executive summary also presents possible 20–40% external-spend reductions over three years. These are targets or prospective opportunities, not achieved market-wide savings.

kp.k: Provider engagement lags client expectations
kp.d: 58% of GCs say providers rarely or never proactively discuss AI benefits. Figure 21 places 48% at initial conversations, 19% with no conversations, 19% incorporating AI into selection criteria, 9% co-developing benefits and just 4% directly experiencing benefits. Deloitte recommends explicit panel and tender criteria, spend analytics, updated billing controls, co-development and strategic insourcing. It argues that proactive firms can shape benefit-sharing discussions and strengthen relationships, whereas reactive firms surrender the terms to clients.
qs: Proactive partners can shape the conversation before the client defines it.
Reactive partners will wait for the client to raise AI

kp.k: Law-firm economics require more than fixed fees
kp.d: Deloitte identifies a tension between fewer hours needed for legal work, protecting revenue and passing efficiency benefits to clients. It argues that changing fee labels alone is insufficient: firms should align AI with commercial strategy, growth, new services, reduced non-billable work, fewer write-offs and matter profitability. Reported build-versus-buy views differ, but Deloitte locates differentiation in institutional knowledge, redesigned workflows, business-model innovation and adoption at scale rather than model strength alone.
qs: The billable hour model becomes significantly harder
alternative fee arrangements and fixed fees.
Growth: using AI to win new client work and expand market
Profitability: prioritising AI to reduce non-billable time

kp.k: Transformation requires sequenced organisational redesign
kp.d: Deloitte recommends three stages: Foundations establishes strategy, leadership, data, governance and adoption; Embedding redesigns practice workflows, integrates knowledge, pilots agents and activates workforce and provider changes; Scaling makes AI structural to the operating model, with advanced analytics, outcome-based relationships and agent governance. Its central prescription is balanced investment in people, process, knowledge and technology, not merely layering AI over existing work. The report’s claims about which organisations will lead by 2030 are strategic predictions.
qs: not just overlaying AI onto existing ways of working.
a structural component of its operating model.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Deloitte presents AI as a structural change to legal delivery, staffing and commercial relationships, with adoption already widespread but much of the expected value still ahead.
pts.d: Adoption and investment: Deloitte reports that 79% of surveyed legal departments increased AI investment, with an average increase of 67% among those reporting an increase. Figure 5 places 31% in initial deployment, 30% in scaling deployment and 10% in fully embedded use, versus 2% with no adoption. The report compares this with 76% reporting no adoption in its 2024 survey. Technology and infrastructure dominates investment, while transformation and training receive less emphasis. Productivity and capability: respondents expect AI to save or automate an average of 28% of legal department work within two to three years, led by contracts and commercial at 34%, legal operations at 32%, and regulatory and compliance at 29%. Deloitte expects benefits beyond faster document work: broader risk coverage, data-led advice, contract intelligence and predictive litigation analysis. Agentic AI is presented as extending automation into multistep work, including business queries, triage and contract review; 61% report experimenting or piloting it. Workforce: 58% expect broadly unchanged team size but different composition, seniority or skills; 20% expect smaller teams, compared with 10% in 2024. Deloitte predicts reduced demand and salaries for routine junior roles, greater value for legal engineers and expert senior lawyers, and movement from a staffing pyramid toward a leaner diamond with a broader hybrid-skilled middle. Its illustrative future department includes AI agents, AI-native lawyers, hybrid engineers/lawyers, legal engineers, knowledge engineers and legal operations; this is Deloitte's scenario rather than a measured staffing forecast. It anticipates more sophisticated residual human work and new training pathways based on simulation, rotations and demonstrated competence. Pricing and sourcing: 85% of respondents expect AI to change law-firm pricing to at least a moderate extent; the expected hourly-priced share falls from 72% to 44% in two to three years. Deloitte identifies potential external-spend reductions of 20–40% through benefit-sharing with firms and insourcing. It predicts competitive advantages for firms that redesign delivery and proactively discuss benefits with clients. ALSP and nearshore/offshore sourcing expectations are mixed, with more respondents anticipating increases than decreases. Deloitte also argues that adequate internal AI capability can support bringing previously outsourced work back in-house.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of a 121-person corporate legal leadership survey, qualitative law-firm interviews and Deloitte client cases; forecasts and recommendations are distinguished from reported outcomes.
pts.d: The methodology specifies an online questionnaire administered in April–May 2026 to 121 senior legal leaders, including General Counsels, Heads of Legal, Legal Operations Directors and Managing Legal Counsels. The sample covers departments below 25 FTE through above 200 FTE, several industries, and the Americas, APAC, EMEA and UK & Ireland. Deloitte conducted the survey in partnership with RSGI and states that the analysis and commentary are its own. Law-firm perspectives are supplemented by informal interviews, rather than a separately quantified law-firm survey. Adoption, spending, anticipated automation, future staffing and pricing figures are respondent reports or expectations, not benchmark measurements of AI performance. The supplied methodology does not establish that the 2024 and 2026 samples are a matched panel. Deloitte's client cases report: deployment to 1,200 financial-services legal professionals, initial adoption above 75%, and 5–8% productivity across drafting/review capabilities; an AmLaw30 firm's AI-assistant adoption above 85% following a strategy and literacy programme; and an insurance claims redesign associated with €6 million annual external-spend reduction. A contract-intelligence case concerns a repository exceeding one million agreements but supplies no quantified productivity outcome. Salesforce's case describes live agents, prospective capabilities, governance reviews and an Agent Manager role; it does not provide a quantified reduction in requests. Deloitte's broader enterprise report supplies cross-domain context, including anticipated growth in agentic adoption, low mature agent-governance prevalence and the claim that 84% have not redesigned roles around AI; that last statistic should not be treated as a result of this legal survey. Predictions about salaries, the diamond staffing model, future workforce shares and 2030 winners rely on Deloitte's analysis and experience, with technology and customer-service analogies rather than dedicated legal labour-market measurements. Some summaries vary internally: the body and Figure 5 distinguish 61% in initial/scaling deployment from a further 10% fully embedded; the executive summary uses deployment terminology less consistently. Figure 10 also differs from surrounding prose on some expected benefits, so those values should retain their specific attribution.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most quantitative expectations concern the next two to three years after the 2026 survey; Deloitte makes realisation of gains conditional on organisational redesign, capability-building and governance.
pts.d: Current adoption and year-on-year spending refer to the April–May 2026 survey, published in June 2026, with some comparisons to 2024. Automation, transformative use cases, skill changes, sourcing and pricing expectations generally concern the next two to three years. The workforce illustration specifies three years, although the executive-summary heading also refers to three to five years. The executive summary presents possible external-spend reductions over three years, while Section 4 describes some GCs' 20–40% cost-reduction targets over two to three years. The roadmap extends to the legal landscape of 2030. Conditions: Deloitte argues that software procurement alone is insufficient; sustained value requires balanced investment in people, knowledge/data, process redesign and technology, along with clear ownership, metrics and leadership. Only 24% report defined use-case QA frameworks, rising to 33% among high-maturity respondents, and Deloitte says this gap becomes more consequential as workflows and agents become more advanced. High maturity means scaling deployment or fully embedded adoption. Half of that group, versus 38% overall, anticipate transformative direct-to-client AI advice within two to three years; Deloitte notes continuing human-in-the-loop caution and the importance of guardrails. Meeting growing demand without additional or potentially with fewer staff is conditional on adopting AI and reshaping the workforce appropriately. Cost-oriented organisations are more likely to anticipate headcount reductions. Buy/build choices depend on enterprise capability, security requirements, procurement constraints and differentiation objectives; consumption-based AI charges require active cost governance. ALSP insourcing depends on sufficient internal investment and capability, while shared services or ALSP investment can instead favour outsourcing. The training, salary and diamond-model predictions have no precise quantified deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source primarily concerns corporate legal buyers and their providers, with differentiated effects on junior lawyers, senior specialists, hybrid professionals and business users.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments and their GCs face pressure to demonstrate ROI, maintain or reduce budgets, support growing demand and decide whether freed capacity should fund insourcing, more strategic work or fewer staff. Government/public-sector respondents in this sample all favoured broadly stable size with changed composition; smaller-team expectations were most common in financial services, chemicals/agriculture and technology. Contracts/commercial and other high-volume document workflows show the strongest automation expectations, while antitrust/competition has a lower anticipated rate of 19%. Internal business users gain self-service, faster access to contract information and potentially direct AI advice. Law firms face fewer chargeable hours for equivalent output, client pressure for pricing transparency and benefit-sharing, and opportunities to compete on speed, quality, relationships, new services and profitability. Deloitte reports that 58% of GCs say providers rarely or never initiate AI-benefit discussions and only 4% have directly experienced benefits, framing proactive collaboration as a potential differentiator. Paralegals, trainees and junior associates face reduced demand for routine work and disruption of traditional learning-by-doing. Senior lawyers with expertise and client relationships are presented as relatively well positioned, while legal engineers, knowledge engineers and hybrid roles gain importance. Legal operations expands toward transformation and outside-counsel management as routine activity is automated. Future entrants may follow legal-engineering pathways rather than conventional traineeships. ALSPs and managed-service providers may receive more work where their multi-client AI investments offer advantages, or lose work where buyers can internalise it; Figure 18 shows 45% expecting increased ALSP/managed-service use, 22% decreased use and 21% finding it too early to assess. These claims concern enterprise legal service delivery, not demonstrated access-to-justice gains for underserved individuals.
